nodes.label: The schema-aware guidance engine (spec)
Survey: no library exposes an XSD component model
nodes.rationale: libxml2 keeps particles in private headers so binding harder does not help; code generators discard sequence ordering, occurrence bounds, choice structure and substitution groups, and JSON Schema cannot express xs:sequence ordering at all; real component models (Xerces2-J XSModel, Saxon-EE) are Java/.NET and would mean multi-megabyte payloads.

nodes.label: Xerces XSCMValidator.whatCanGoHere precedent
nodes.rationale: Xerces2-J's three-way split (XSDFACM, XSAllCM, XSEmptyCM) shows the approach is standard rather than invented; Xerces is Apache-2.0 so reading it is legally clean, but reimplement from the published algorithms rather than transliterating.

nodes.label: Glushkov position automaton
nodes.rationale: For 1-unambiguous expressions the Glushkov automaton is already deterministic — no subset construction, no NFA state sets, runtime state is a single integer plus a small counter vector. UPA therefore collapses the implementation cost and makes the forward run O(n).

nodes.label: Unique Particle Attribution and graceful UPA degradation
nodes.rationale: Real schemas violate UPA, including hand-written ones a beginner will bring. Detect at compile time, surface as a schema warning, and degrade the runtime to NFA state sets — refusing to open a slightly-broken schema is a product failure for our user.

nodes.label: whatCanGoHere: forward run intersected with backward co-reachability
nodes.rationale: The backward sweep is what makes the query genuinely position-aware rather than merely 'children allowed by this type': a suggestion is only offered if the material already present after the caret can still be completed.

nodes.label: Single backward co-reachability sweep for every gap
nodes.rationale: One sweep from n down to 0 yields CoReach_i for every i simultaneously, so all insertion gaps in a parent cost O(n*|states|) together rather than per gap. Memoised on (contentModelId, hash(childNameSequence)).

nodes.label: Numeric occurrence: unbounded / unroll / counting hybrid
nodes.rationale: Unrolling finite bounds is exactly correct and trivially debuggable but blows up, so it is gated on a ~2,000 total-position budget with a counting automaton above it. In real schemas maxOccurs is essentially always 1 or unbounded, so instrument the budget rather than assuming.

nodes.label: AllContentModel: xs:all is a bitset, not an automaton
nodes.rationale: XSD 1.0 restricts xs:all so heavily that a seen-members bitset is simpler and faster than the automaton path, mirroring Xerces's XSAllCM. XSD 1.1 relaxes all of it, so the bitset generalises to a counter vector behind a version flag sharing the same interface.

nodes.label: Substitution groups as symbol matchers, never expansion
nodes.rationale: On UBL or GML a head can have hundreds of members: expansion explodes the position count and destroys the 1-unambiguity that gave you a DFA. Keep one position per particle carrying matchesElement(qname).

nodes.label: Effective content models (extension, restriction, xsi:type)
nodes.rationale: Restriction-legality checking is where most homegrown XSD implementations stall, and it affects schema authoring correctness rather than instance editing — so v1 skips it and routes it to a later schema-lint mode. xsi:type gets a first-class Type dropdown because 'is this a Domestic or an International address?' is exactly the question a beginner needs asked of them.

nodes.label: Wildcards: processContents drives the UI directly
nodes.rationale: strict gives a picker of global elements, lax adds a custom-name escape, skip gives a free-text box with a 'not checked' badge. Wildcard suggestions must rank below named elements in a separate section or a beginner drowns in noise.

nodes.label: Required-and-missing as a shortest-path BFS
nodes.rationale: BFS from the final state to the nearest accepting state, preferring concrete declarations over wildcards, yields the literal ordered list powering 'Add all 3 missing children'. mandatoryAt(i) is sound and cheap by re-testing completion with each candidate removed from the alphabet.

nodes.label: Tri-state validity badging (red / amber / green)
nodes.rationale: Falls straight out of the automaton with no extra machinery: red when the forward run dies, amber when it survives but is non-accepting, green when accepting and all value checks pass.

nodes.label: Quick fixes from error-tolerant alignment
nodes.rationale: When the prefix already fails is precisely the moment a beginner needs the most help, so do not emit 'invalid content'. Each edit operation maps one-to-one onto a quick fix (substitution to rename, deletion to remove, insertion to add, transposition to swap). Build the one algorithm deliberately rather than accreting per-error heuristics.

nodes.label: buildSkeleton and placeholder provenance
nodes.rationale: Every auto-filled value carries unfilled: true so the UI shows amber 'needs your input' rather than a green tick. Silently generating a document full of plausible fake data that validates is the worst possible outcome for a beginner — it teaches them the tool's approval is meaningless. Guarded by a type-recurrence stack, a ~500 node budget and a depth cap.

nodes.label: widgetFor(simpleTypeDef) decision table
nodes.rationale: Written as an explicit table rather than a heuristic because this is where the beginner actually spends their time.

nodes.label: XSD regex is not JavaScript regex (types/xsdRegex.ts)
nodes.rationale: XSD patterns are implicitly anchored, support character-class subtraction which JS lacks entirely, carry the \i \I \c \C XML-name escapes, and lack backreferences and lazy quantifiers. Treating them as interchangeable silently corrupts validation. Paired with a deterministic string generator over the same AST because the example is worth more to a beginner than the pattern.

nodes.label: describeParticle / describeType — the guaranteed fallback
nodes.rationale: Most schemas a beginner meets have no documentation at all, so synthesising plain English from the components themselves does more for the beginner experience than all the annotation plumbing combined. Annotation content is mixed and frequently contains embedded XHTML, so render as sanitised HTML rather than flattened text.

nodes.label: Pluggable xs:appinfo interpreter registry
nodes.rationale: Real-world enterprise schemas routinely encode presentation metadata in appinfo, and this is the escape hatch that makes them look good.

nodes.label: Diagnostic interface
nodes.rationale: Produce diagnostics structurally and never parse validator message strings; plain English is rendered from structured params with the spec-ese kept behind 'show details'.

nodes.label: QuickFix interface
nodes.rationale: apply() returns a Command so fixes are atomically undoable; the interface is designed now so SQF operations map onto it cleanly rather than needing a parallel mechanism later.

nodes.label: Badge roll-up and incremental revalidation
nodes.rationale: A problem here (solid dot) is rendered distinguishably from a problem inside (ring) so the user can drill down from the root; revalidation is debounced at ~150ms and incremental, with document-global constraints run in the worker on idle.

nodes.label: Error taxonomy — 20 classes, each with a plain-English rewrite and a fix
Schematron Quick Fixes (SQF)
nodes.rationale: Lets schema authors ship domain-specific one-click fixes with their rules, which no browser-based editor currently offers and which fits the teach-the-beginner thesis exactly. Scoped as a stretch item.

nodes.label: Schema-less mode: infer, but never disguise a guess as a rule
nodes.rationale: Every hint carries source: 'schema' | 'inferred' | 'heuristic' and the UI labels inferred suggestions 'learned from your document', never 'required'. A beginner must always be able to tell a rule from a guess.

nodes.label: SOA to SORE content-model inference
nodes.rationale: Roughly 300 LOC, essentially what Trang does; the same machinery powers 'Generate an XSD from this document' and from N documents.

nodes.label: Guidance degrades; the tool never does
nodes.rationale: Every editing operation stays available on an unschema'd node; four partial-schema situations get four distinct badges, including a search of ancestors and siblings for a parent whose content model does accept a rejected element.

nodes.label: Namespace mismatch deserves its own diagnostic
nodes.rationale: By far the most common way a beginner's document fails, and the raw validator reports an unhelpful 'no declaration found'. Detect it before generic undeclared-element handling by testing whether the local name matches a declaration in some other namespace. elementFormDefault="unqualified" is the classic trap and looks like a bug in the tool.

nodes.label: OASIS XML Catalogs for resolution
nodes.rationale: So the app works offline, behind corporate firewalls, and without fetching arbitrary URLs at load time.

nodes.label: Scope and sequencing (P1-P10), simple-type compiler is the sleeper
nodes.rationale: A pragmatic v1 dropping identity constraints, restriction-legality checking and the rarer facets lands near 3,500 LOC. Sequence P6 (particle to automaton) and P9 (query API) early — they are the product.

nodes.label: Lazy per-type content-model compilation and IndexedDB persistence
nodes.rationale: UBL is ~2MB across many files with thousands of type definitions, so compiling everything at load is wasted work; compiled models persist keyed by a hash of the concatenated sources so reopening is instant and offline.

nodes.label: Instrument compile time, position counts, unroll-budget hits, UPA violations
nodes.rationale: Those four metrics tell you whether the design assumptions survive contact with real schemas.
